text: The user is considering getting a bird feeder for their backyard and is unsure which seed to use, asking for an all-purpose seed mix that will attract a variety of birds.
The user attended a bird watching workshop at the local Audubon society about a month before 25 May 2023 (around late April 2023) and learned a lot about attracting birds to their yard.

The assistant recommended five food types for an all-purpose bird seed mix: black oil sunflower seeds (high in fat and protein, favoured by cardinals, finches and sparrows), Nyjer seed (thistle, favoured by finches, sparrows and other small birds), safflower seeds (less likely to attract squirrels, favoured by cardinals, finches and doves), suet (attracts woodpeckers, nuthatches and chickadees), and dried fruit and nuts such as cranberries, cherries, peanuts and hazelnuts (attract blue jays, woodpeckers and robins).
The assistant suggested an all-purpose seed mix containing 20-30% black oil sunflower seeds, 20-30% Nyjer seed, 20-30% safflower seeds, 10-20% suet, and 10-20% fruit and nuts.

The assistant named Audubon Park, Perky-Pet, Wild Birds Unlimited and Droll Yankees as popular brands offering good all-purpose bird seed mixes, and advised choosing seed that is fresh and stored properly so it stays viable and attractive to birds.

The assistant advised placing the bird feeder where it gets morning sun and is protected from strong winds and predators, keeping it clean to prevent mold and bacteria, providing water such as a birdbath or pond, and planting native vegetation that offers shelter, food and nesting sites.
The user is also thinking of buying a birdbath to go with the feeder and asked for recommendations on a birdbath that is easy to clean and maintain.

The assistant recommended birdbaths that are shallow (around 1-2 inches deep) with a wide basin, have smooth non-porous surfaces such as ceramic, glass or plastic, include built-in drainage holes or a removable plug, and have a lightweight, easy-to-lift design.

The assistant named Bird Brain, Perky-Pet and Droll Yankees as birdbath brands that fit those criteria, and advised avoiding concrete or wood birdbaths, placing the birdbath in partial shade to reduce algae and heat, and cleaning it with a soft brush and mild soap while refilling it with fresh water every 2-3 days.
The user is interested in buying a field guide to learn about different bird species and their habits, and asked for a field guide that is good for beginners.

The assistant recommended four beginner field guides: the National Audubon Society Field Guide to Birds (over 800 species, with range maps and excellent photographs), the Sibley Guide to Birds by David Allen Sibley (over 900 species and more detailed), the Peterson Field Guide to Birds (over 750 species, trusted for over 70 years), and the Kaufman Field Guide to Birds by Kenn Kaufman (over 750 species, with a user-friendly layout).

The assistant recommended the mobile apps Merlin Bird ID, iBird Pro and Audubon Birds for identifying birds from photos and descriptions, the online resources AllAboutBirds, BirdLife International and the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, and joining a local birding group.
The user has been listening to bird call recordings on their phone to identify birds by ear and asked for tips on improving this skill.

The assistant advised the user to start with common birds such as American Robin, Northern Cardinal, Blue Jay and Mourning Dove, listen to recordings repeatedly, practise active listening to pitch, tone, rhythm and volume, and compare similar-sounding species such as Chipping Sparrow and Clay-colored Sparrow.

The assistant listed bird call learning resources: the Cornell Lab of Ornithology's All About Birds website and Merlin Bird ID app, the Audubon Society's Birds of a Feather app, the Sibley Guide to Birds app, Xeno-canto (an online database of bird calls and sounds), and forums such as BirdForum and Reddit's r/birding.
The user plans to attend a birder's meetup the weekend of 27-28 May 2023 (described as next weekend from 25 May 2023), which includes a guided walk at a local nature preserve.

The assistant advised meetup attendees to wear comfortable walking shoes and dress in layers, bring sun protection, insect repellent and a hat, bring binoculars and a field guide, arrive early to meet the group leader, stay on designated trails, keep noise down, and take notes and photos to help with identification later.

The assistant suggested questions to ask the group leader or other participants on the guided walk, such as the best way to identify a species, the habitat and behaviour of a bird, how to distinguish similar species, and the most interesting birding experience they have had.
The user is trying to get back on track with a reading goal of 50 books by the end of 2023 and asked how many books per month they need to read to reach it.

The assistant explained that the monthly target is found by dividing the books still needed by the months left in the year, and gave an example for a September start with four months left: 50 books / 4 months = 12.5 books per month.
The user has already read 12 books so far in 2023 and asked for non-fiction books that are not too dense, having been enjoying 'Sapiens' but finding it really slow going.
The assistant recalculated the target as 50 - 12 = 38 books remaining and, assuming it was September with four months left, 38 / 4 = 9.5 books per month, or around 9-10 books per month.

The assistant recommended five accessible non-fiction books: 'The Devil in the White City' by Erik Larson (the 1893 Chicago World's Fair and serial killer H.H. Holmes), 'Bad Blood' by John Carreyrou (the rise and fall of Theranos), 'The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks' by Rebecca Skloot, 'Just Mercy' by Bryan Stevenson, and 'The Power of Habit' by Charles Duhigg.

The user asked for self-help or personal development books backed by scientific research rather than inspirational stories or anecdotes, focused on practical advice for improving daily habits and productivity.

The assistant recommended ten self-help books: 'Atomic Habits' by James Clear, 'Deep Work' by Cal Newport, 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People' by Stephen Covey, 'Mindset: The New Psychology of Success' by Carol S. Dweck, 'The Power of Now' by Eckhart Tolle, 'Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience' by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, 'The Happiness Advantage' by Shawn Achor, 'Mini Habits' by Stephen Guise, 'The Productivity Project' by Chris Bailey, and 'The Willpower Instinct' by Kelly McGonigal.
The user is interested in 'Atomic Habits' and 'Deep Work' and asked how these books could help them increase their reading speed and retain more information.

The assistant said 'Atomic Habits' can build a consistent reading habit through habit stacking (attaching reading to an existing routine such as after breakfast or before bed), an identity-based habit of seeing oneself as a reader, starting small with 10-15 minutes a day, and implementation intentions such as 'If it's Monday, I'll read for 20 minutes during my lunch break'.

The assistant said 'Deep Work' can improve reading sessions through a distraction-free environment, scheduled deep reading blocks, the Pomodoro Technique (25 minutes of focus followed by a 5-minute break), and active reading that involves taking notes, asking questions and summarising the material.

The user is on page 250 of 'The Nightingale' by Kristin Hannah, really getting into it, and asked for a plan applying 'Atomic Habits' and 'Deep Work' to schedule reading sessions, eliminate distractions and practise active reading.

The assistant's reading plan suggested a daily goal of 30-40 pages or 30-60 minutes, a consistent time such as early morning, lunch or evening, and treating reading sessions as non-negotiable appointments written in a calendar or set as phone reminders.

The assistant's plan for eliminating distractions included a quiet, comfortable reading spot such as a corner at home, a library or a bookstore, silencing phones and other devices with apps such as Freedom, SelfControl or Moment, and avoiding multitasking while reading.

The assistant's plan for active reading included keeping a reading journal in Evernote or Simplenote to note quotes, character developments, themes and questions, summarising and reflecting after each session, and tracking progress with Habitica or HabitBull.

The assistant's example plan was 30 minutes of reading during the lunch break from 12:00 to 12:30 PM on weekdays and 60 minutes of reading from 9:00 to 10:00 AM on weekends, with notes taken and main events summarised after each session.

The user has been tracking reading habits in a spreadsheet and asked how many pages per day they need to read to reach 50 books by the end of 2023, having already read 12 books. The user has just got back to reading 'The Nightingale', which has 440 pages.

The assistant estimated 38 remaining books at an assumed average of 400 pages per book, based on the length of 'The Nightingale', giving about 15,200 pages, and with about 154 days left until 31 December, roughly 99 pages per day.

The user has been reading a mix of dense non-fiction and graphic novels, has been reading 'Sapiens' at a pace of 10-20 pages a week, and thinks their reading speed is slower than the 99 pages per day estimate.

The assistant assumed 15 pages per week, about 2.14 pages per day, which would take about 7,099 days to read 15,200 pages, and then suggested reading around 46 days' worth of the user's usual reading, approximately 92-100 pages, every day.
The user found that pace too ambitious and asked for other options, such as increasing the number of days dedicated to reading or finding ways to speed up their reading.

The assistant offered two options: adding 2-3 more reading days a week for 5-6 reading days in total, or improving reading speed through better comprehension, active reading, short reading breaks, audiobooks, e-books or graphic novels, and 25-minute timed sessions, aiming for 3-4 pages per day, with a hybrid of both also suggested.
The user plans to increase the number of days spent reading and to alternate graphic novels and manga, which are quicker to get through, with their denser non-fiction books.

The assistant endorsed alternating graphic novels and manga with denser non-fiction, suggesting 2-3 days of non-fiction followed by 1-2 days of graphic novels or manga, dedicated catch-up days for page count, or a 'reading sandwich' of graphic novel, non-fiction, then graphic novel.

The user is looking for healthy meal ideas for busy weekdays and says they have been relying on food delivery a lot, having had Domino's Pizza three times in the week of 15 May 2023.

The assistant suggested quick healthy breakfasts for busy weekdays: overnight oats, avocado toast on whole-grain bread topped with salt, pepper and a fried egg if time allows, and a Greek yogurt parfait with granola and favourite berries.

The assistant suggested quick healthy lunches: salad jars layering greens, vegetables, protein such as chicken, tuna or tofu, and a simple vinaigrette; whole-grain wraps with roasted turkey, avocado, lettuce and tomato; and a big batch of weekend lentil soup served with a whole-grain sandwich or salad.

The assistant suggested quick healthy dinners and snacks: one-pot pasta with vegetables and chicken, shrimp or tofu, slow cooker stews or chili started in the morning, quesadillas of shredded chicken, beans and vegetables on whole-grain tortillas, fresh fruit and nuts, energy balls, and hummus with vegetables.

The assistant advised meal prepping on one weekend day, planning the week's meals with a grocery list to avoid last-minute takeout, and packing lunch the night before or the morning of to avoid relying on delivery.
The user likes the overnight oats idea but is not a big fan of nuts, and asked for other toppings to use instead.

The assistant suggested nut-free overnight oat toppings: fresh berries, sliced bananas or diced apples, dried cranberries, apricots or raisins, chia or flaxseeds, unsweetened coconut flakes, cinnamon, cocoa powder or vanilla, honey, maple syrup or fruit preserves, Greek yogurt, peanut or sunflower seed butter, tahini or hemp seed butter, and shredded coconut or shaved dark chocolate.
The user likes the idea of adding chia or flaxseeds to overnight oats but is not sure how to incorporate them and asked for a simple recipe to get started.

The assistant gave a basic chia overnight oats recipe: 1/2 cup rolled oats, 1/2 cup unsweetened almond milk or milk of choice, 1 tablespoon chia seeds, optional 1 tablespoon honey or maple syrup, a pinch of salt and toppings, refrigerated for at least 4 hours or overnight (8-10 hours), with a creamier texture achieved by using less chia or adding a splash more milk.
The assistant said the flaxseed version replaces the 1 tablespoon of chia seeds with 1 tablespoon of ground flaxseeds, which have a slightly nutty flavour and a coarser texture than chia seeds.

The user is thinking of trying the flaxseed version and asked whether a regular blender is enough to grind flaxseeds or whether a special grinder is needed. The assistant said a coffee grinder, a high-powered blender pulsed in short bursts, a food processor or a mortar and pestle can all grind flaxseeds, advising grinding just before use in small batches because ground flaxseed can go rancid.

The user decided to try a coffee grinder for the flaxseeds, and the assistant confirmed a coffee grinder works perfectly for this. The user also planned to make a batch of quinoa and black bean salad with grilled chicken for lunch in the week of 22 May 2023 and asked how to make it more flavourful.

The assistant suggested flavour boosters for the quinoa and black bean salad: a cilantro lime dressing (fresh cilantro, lime juice, olive oil, garlic and a pinch of salt), roasted bell peppers, onions and jalapenos, grilled pineapple, avocado crema with lime, salt and cumin, feta crumbles, toasted and ground cumin and coriander, and diced chipotle peppers in adobo sauce.

The assistant also suggested a chipotle-lime or fajita-style grilled chicken breast, chopped parsley, basil or cilantro in the quinoa mixture, tri-colour or red quinoa for a nuttier flavour, and chopped hard-boiled eggs, diced tomatoes or sliced black olives for a more substantial salad.
The user likes the cilantro lime dressing idea and plans to try it, and asked how to cook chicken breast more flavourfully, as the user's grilled chicken has sometimes turned out a bit dry.

The assistant gave grilling tips for juicy chicken breast: marinate in olive oil, an acid such as lime juice or vinegar, and spices for 30 minutes to an hour; brine in 1 tablespoon of salt per 1 cup of water for 30 minutes to an hour; pound to an even thickness; grill over medium-low heat of 325-350 F; avoid pressing down; cook to 165 F; and rest for 5-10 minutes before slicing.

The assistant suggested pan-searing, oven roasting with onions, carrots and celery, or poaching in broth as alternatives if grilling keeps producing dry chicken breast, and listed chipotle lime, herby and Korean-style gochujang chicken as flavourful recipes.
The user is looking for quick and easy recipe ideas for weeknights and mentioned that their weekends have been all about Uber Eats lately, which has been a lifesaver.

The assistant suggested one-pot weeknight meals: chicken fajita pasta with bell peppers, onions and fajita seasoning, quick chicken and rice with vegetables in broth, and lentil soup with onions, garlic, carrots, lentils, broth and diced tomatoes.

The assistant suggested 30-minute meals: taco night with pre-cooked ground beef, shredded cheese, lettuce and tomatoes; an omelette with eggs, cheese and vegetables such as bell peppers, onions and mushrooms; and baked seasoned chicken breasts with broccoli, carrots and sweet potatoes.

The assistant suggested pantry-staple meals: a grilled cheese and tomato sandwich, spaghetti with marinara and sauteed cherry tomatoes and spinach, and black bean and corn tacos using canned black beans, frozen corn and store-bought taco seasoning. It also suggested meal-prep ideas: slow cooker chili, a roasted whole chicken with vegetables, and mason jar salads.
The user plans to try the Chicken Fajita Pasta and asked for healthy snack options, as the user wants to make healthier choices than relying on Uber Eats for convenience.

The assistant suggested fresh snacks: baby carrots with hummus, fresh fruit salad of grapes, berries and citrus, cucumber slices with guacamole, and apple slices with peanut butter. It also suggested protein snacks: hard-boiled eggs (boil a dozen on the weekend), and Greek yogurt with nuts and berries.

The assistant suggested whole-grain and other snacks: whole-grain crackers with avocado, oatmeal energy balls, whole-grain toast with banana and honey, homemade trail mix, air-popped popcorn, and dark chocolate-dipped fruit. It advised keeping snacks to 100-200 calories per serving.
The user asked for meal prep container recommendations because they want to start meal prepping for the week and do not know what containers to use.

The assistant recommended glass containers (Pyrex, Anchor Hocking or OXO), stainless steel containers (S'well, Hydro Flask or Klean Kanteen), and BPA-free plastic containers made from Tritan or polypropylene (Rubbermaid, Glad or Ziploc) as top meal prep container options.

The assistant said to consider meal prep containers with portion control markings, airtight seals, stackability, microwave-safe and dishwasher-safe construction, and listed mason jars and reused takeout containers as budget-friendly options.
The user is considering getting a cookbook stand to make cooking and following recipes easier and asked for recommendations.

The assistant recommended the OXO Good Grips Cookbook Stand (sturdy, adjustable, non-slip base), the KitchenAid Cookbook Stand (adjustable height and soft-grip surface), and the Cuisinart Cookbook Stand (compact and suited to small kitchens), with budget options the Amazon Basics Cookbook Stand and the Umbra Cookbook Stand.
The user has a bunch of cookbooks and online recipes and wants to consolidate them and make them easier to access, and asked for good apps for organising and tracking recipes.

The assistant recommended recipe apps: Paprika Recipe Manager (iOS, Android, Windows; tagging, meal planning, grocery lists and nutritional analysis), Yummly (iOS, Android), BigOven (iOS, Android; over 200,000 recipes), Kitchen Stories (iOS, Android), and Recipe Keeper (iOS, Android). It also named Evernote, OneNote and Google Keep as note-taking alternatives.
The user is interested in learning about meal planning and grocery lists and asked for examples of how to plan meals for the week and create a grocery list based on those meals.

The assistant gave an example weekly meal plan: Monday chicken fajitas with bell peppers and onions; Tuesday baked salmon with roasted vegetables and quinoa; Wednesday lentil soup with crusty bread; Thursday grilled chicken breasts with roasted sweet potatoes and green beans; Friday pizza night with homemade crust; Saturday breakfast for dinner with scrambled eggs, sausage and pancakes; and Sunday slow cooker chili with ground beef and vegetables.

The assistant said to build a grocery list by writing down all ingredients for each meal, checking pantry staples already at home, organising the list by category such as produce, meat, dairy and grains, and buying in bulk or planning around sales, and gave an example list covering these categories.

The user is looking for healthy lunch recipe ideas and says they have been really busy lately and relying on food delivery, including a new service called Fresh Fusion, which offers great pre-made meals.

The assistant suggested healthy lunch salads, sandwiches, wraps and soups: a grilled chicken and avocado salad with citrus vinaigrette, a quinoa and black bean salad with balsamic vinaigrette, a turkey and avocado wrap with hummus, a grilled chicken and veggie sandwich with sweet potato fries, lentil soup, and tomato and spinach soup.

The assistant suggested global and quick lunch options: Korean-style chicken and veggies with gochujang, soy sauce and honey served with brown or cauliflower rice; an Indian-style lentil and veggie bowl; overnight oats; and a quesadilla of shredded veggies, cheese and beans. It advised balancing Fresh Fusion meals with home-cooked meals and checking their nutritional content and ingredient quality.
The user made a quinoa and black bean salad recently and asked for a healthy dinner option that is quick to make and does not require many ingredients.

The assistant recommended One-Pot Pesto Pasta with Cherry Tomatoes and Spinach: 10 minutes prep and 15 minutes cook (25 minutes total), using 1 cup whole-grain pasta, 1/4 cup pesto, 1 cup halved cherry tomatoes, 1 cup fresh spinach leaves, optional 1/2 cup grated mozzarella, salt, pepper and 1 tablespoon olive oil.

The assistant's pesto pasta method was to cook the pasta in salted water, then add pesto, cherry tomatoes and spinach to the same pot for 2-3 minutes, drain and return the pasta, toss, and season with salt, pepper and olive oil. It noted the dish is healthy because whole-grain pasta provides fibre, and tomatoes and spinach add vitamin C, lycopene, iron, and vitamins A and K.

The user has all the ingredients for the pesto pasta at home and planned to try it that evening, 20 May 2023. The user also asked for healthy breakfast options that can be meal-prepped on the weekends.

The assistant suggested eight weekend meal-prep breakfasts: overnight oats, breakfast burritos, muffin tin frittatas (refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze), smoothie packs of frozen fruit, veg and milk or yogurt, avocado toast mixture (refrigerate up to 3 days), quiche (up to 5 days), chia seed pudding, and breakfast casseroles (up to 5 days).
The user chose to try breakfast burritos and said they have been wanting to meal prep more on the weekends, finding this a convenient and healthy option.

The assistant gave breakfast burrito meal-prep tips: batch cook scrambled eggs, sausage or bacon and black beans on the weekend, use whole-grain tortillas, portion fillings, wrap burritos individually and freeze for up to 3 months, and reheat until steaming hot.
The user asked whether the best way to reheat frozen breakfast burritos is in the microwave or the oven.

The assistant said to microwave a frozen burrito wrapped in a microwave-safe paper towel on high for 1-2 minutes, rotating it after the first minute and heating in 30-second increments if needed. For the oven, preheat to 350 F (180 C), wrap in foil and bake for 15-20 minutes, checking and rotating after 10 minutes. It said to reach an internal temperature of 165 F (74 C), and that broiling for 1-2 minutes adds crispness.
The user is thinking of adding new ingredients to their breakfast burritos and asked for unique fillings or toppings to boost flavour and nutrition.

The assistant suggested unique burrito fillings: roasted sweet potatoes, Brussels sprouts or broccoli; chorizo or Korean chorizo with gochujang; sauteed mushroom duxelles; black beans with cumin and coriander; and grilled pineapple with scrambled eggs and cheese.

The assistant suggested burrito toppings: avocado salsa, pickled onions, cilantro lime crema made from Greek yogurt, lime juice, cilantro and salt, sliced radishes, feta cheese, kimchi, sliced jalapenos, fresh cilantro, sliced scallions and guacamole.
